whoIsThisFor.heading: Who is the Marketing Cloud Engagement Foundations exam for?

personas.label: People new to Marketing Cloud Engagement
personas.description: You have a few weeks or months in the tool and want a credential that proves you can find your way around it.

personas.label: Email marketers moving off another platform
personas.description: You know campaigns and deliverability from Mailchimp, Braze or HubSpot and need the Salesforce vocabulary for the same ideas.

personas.label: Admins who inherited the marketing org
personas.description: Someone has to own Marketing Cloud and it turned out to be you. This covers the ground you are expected to know.

examDifficulty.heading: Is the Marketing Cloud Engagement Foundations Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: This is one of the gentler Salesforce exams. It is aimed at people with up to six months in Marketing Cloud Engagement and it checks that you can navigate the studios, send an email properly, tell a list apart from a data extension and read a tracking report. There is no coding and no data architecture.
bullets: 40 questions in 70 minutes. Over a minute and a half each, which is comfortable for questions this size.
Passing score is around 62%, so roughly 26 right out of 40.
Breadth, not depth. You need to know what each studio is for rather than how to build anything complicated in it.
$75, which is a quarter of what the role-based exams cost. The cheapest way to find out whether Marketing Cloud suits you.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: You are ready when you can log into a Marketing Cloud org and, without clicking around hunting for things. Build a data extension, create an email in Content Builder, send it to a segment and then find the open and click numbers afterwards. If any of those four still takes you a while, spend another week in the tool.

examFormat.heading: Marketing Cloud Engagement Foundations Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: Proctored online or at a test centre. The shape of it:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Somewhere around a third of the questions put you in a situation rather than asking for a definition. Usually it is a choice of audience source for a send, or a tracking number you have to interpret.
bestWayToPass: Spend the time in the tool, not in notes. Marketing Cloud has an unusual interface and the exam assumes you have used it. A free trial or a work org beats any amount of reading.

Get lists versus data extensions straight. This single distinction sits behind more questions than any other topic. Lists are the old subscriber model; data extensions are tables you define, and almost everything modern uses them.

Send a real email end to end. Build it in Content Builder. Pick an audience, set a send classification. Do a test send, then go and read the tracking. Doing it once teaches you more than five pages about it.
Learn what the bounce types mean. Hard versus soft bounce, and what each one does to the subscriber record, comes up reliably.

certificationCard.description: The entry-level Marketing Cloud Engagement exam. It covers finding your way around the studios, building and sending email from Content Builder, the difference between subscriber lists and data extensions, simple journeys, and reading tracking reports.

keyConcepts.h2: Marketing Cloud Engagement Foundations: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Email Studio and Content Builder
blocks.body: Content Builder is where emails, images and reusable blocks live. You build an email from a template, drop content blocks into its regions, and personalise it with AMPscript or personalisation strings that pull from the sending audience. Two things matter for the exam. First, content is shared: a block edited in one place changes everywhere it is used, which is the point of templates but catches people out. Second, a send needs three pieces to exist before it will go anywhere, an email, an audience, and a send classification that carries the sender profile and delivery profile. If a question describes a send that will not launch, a missing one of those three is usually the reason.

blocks.heading: Lists, Data Extensions and Contact Builder
blocks.body: Marketing Cloud has two generations of audience storage sitting side by side. Subscriber lists are the original model: a flat set of subscribers, each with a subscriber key, plus profile and preference attributes defined once for the whole account. Data extensions are tables you define yourself, with your own columns and a primary key, and they are where serious work happens because you control the fields and can relate them to each other. Contact Builder is the layer above both, where contacts from every channel are linked together by contact key and where you set up data relationships. For the exam: use a list for a simple newsletter, a data extension when you need fields of your own or more than a handful of attributes.

blocks.heading: Automation Studio
blocks.body: Automation Studio runs sequences of activities on a schedule or when a file lands in the FTP folder. The activities you should recognise are imports, SQL queries that write their results into a data extension, file transfers, data extracts, and the send activity itself. The usual pattern in the exam is a nightly automation that imports a file, runs a query to build a segment, then sends to it. Two distinctions are worth holding on to: Automation Studio is batch and scheduled, while Journey Builder reacts to individual contacts over time; and a SQL query here writes into a data extension rather than returning rows to the screen.

blocks.heading: Journey Builder
blocks.body: A journey is a path a single contact travels. It starts from an entry source, usually a data extension or an API event, and then moves the contact through activities: sends, waits, decision splits, updates. Entry is governed by two settings that questions like to probe, how often the journey re-evaluates its entry source, and whether a contact who has been through before is allowed back in. You should also know the difference between a decision split, which routes on data you already hold, and an engagement split, which routes on whether the contact opened or clicked. Journeys are versioned: once one is running you cannot edit it, you create a new version.

blocks.heading: Tracking and Reporting
blocks.body: Every send produces the same core numbers and you need to read them the way the platform defines them. Sent is how many went out, delivered is sent minus bounces, and opens and clicks are counted against delivered. A hard bounce means the address is permanently bad and the subscriber will be marked undeliverable after it happens; a soft bounce is temporary, a full mailbox or a server refusing for now, and the platform will retry. Unsubscribes come back through the profile centre and land on the All Subscribers record, which is why someone who unsubscribes from one list stops receiving everything unless publication lists are in play. Tracking lives per job in Email Studio, with the cross-channel view in Analytics Builder.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Salesforce Marketing Cloud Engagement Foundations Exam
scenarioTips.intro: This exam rewards hands-on familiarity over revision. Most of the questions are things you would know after a month of actually using the platform.

blocks.heading: Know What Each Studio Does
blocks.body: Email, Mobile, Advertising, Journey Builder, Automation Studio, Content Builder, Contact Builder, Analytics Builder. One sentence each on what it is for is enough.

blocks.heading: Lists Versus Data Extensions
blocks.body: The most reliable topic on the exam. Know what each one is, what a subscriber key is, and why a data extension is the right answer for anything with custom fields.

blocks.heading: Walk the Guided Send
blocks.body: Do a real send, including the test send and the send classification. The exam asks about steps in this process more than once.

blocks.heading: Bounce and Unsubscribe Behaviour
blocks.body: Hard versus soft, what happens to the subscriber record, and where an unsubscribe is recorded. Short topic, dependable marks.

blocks.heading: Read a Tracking Report
blocks.body: Know what delivered, open rate, click-through rate and bounce rate are each calculated against. Questions give you numbers and ask what they mean.

sampleQuestions.question: A marketer needs to store 20 custom fields about each customer, including purchase history and loyalty tier, to use in email personalisation. What should they use?
options: A suppression list
A data extension with columns for each field
A publication list
A subscriber list holding the profile attributes
sampleQuestions.explanation: Data extensions let you define your own columns, which is what storing 20 custom fields requires.
whyWrong: Suppression lists hold addresses to exclude from sends.
Publication lists group subscribers for opt-out purposes; they do not store custom fields.
Profile attributes are defined once for the whole account and are not suited to this volume of record-specific data.

sampleQuestions.question: An email send fails to launch. The email and the audience both exist. What is the most likely missing piece?
options: A second data extension
A journey version
An Analytics Builder report
A send classification
sampleQuestions.explanation: A send needs an email, an audience and a send classification, which carries the sender and delivery profiles.
whyWrong: One audience is enough for a send.
Journeys are a separate feature and are not required for an Email Studio send.
Reporting happens after a send and cannot prevent one.

sampleQuestions.question: What happens to a subscriber record after a hard bounce?
options: The subscriber is added to a publication list
The address is marked permanently undeliverable
The platform keeps retrying the send for several days
Nothing, because hard bounces are temporary
sampleQuestions.explanation: A hard bounce means the address does not exist or has permanently rejected mail, so the platform stops sending to it.
whyWrong: Publication lists are for opt-out management, not bounce handling.
Retrying is what happens after a soft bounce.
Soft bounces are the temporary kind; hard bounces are permanent.

sampleQuestions.question: A nightly process must import a file from the FTP folder. Build a segment from it with SQL, then email that segment. Which tool is designed for this?
options: The Journey Builder tool
Contact Builder
Automation Studio
Content Builder
sampleQuestions.explanation: Automation Studio chains scheduled or file-triggered activities such as imports, queries and sends.
whyWrong: Journey Builder moves individual contacts along a path rather than running batch jobs.
Contact Builder manages contact data relationships.
Content Builder stores email content and assets.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the difference between a decision split and an engagement split in a journey?
options: They are the same feature with different names
A decision split is faster
Decision splits use stored data; engagement splits use opens
An engagement split may only ever be used once per journey
sampleQuestions.explanation: Decision splits read attributes you already hold. Engagement splits react to how the contact behaved with a previous send.
whyWrong: They evaluate genuinely different things.
Speed is not the distinction between them.
There is no such single-use restriction.

sampleQuestions.question: A running journey needs a change to one of its email sends. What must the marketer do?
options: Create a new version of the journey
Pause Automation Studio first
Edit the running journey directly in place
Delete the journey and rebuild it
sampleQuestions.explanation: Journeys are versioned, and a running version is locked. Changes go into a new version.
whyWrong: Automation Studio is unrelated to editing a journey.
A running journey cannot be edited directly.
Deleting loses the history and is unnecessary when versioning exists.

sampleQuestions.question: A subscriber clicks unsubscribe in an email. What is the default effect?
options: They are removed from the whole account entirely
Their data extension row is deleted
They are unsubscribed at All Subscribers level
Only that one email is blocked
sampleQuestions.explanation: Unless publication lists are in use, an unsubscribe applies at the All Subscribers level across the account.
whyWrong: The record remains; its status changes.
Unsubscribing does not delete stored data.
A single-email opt-out is not the default behaviour.

sampleQuestions.question: An email template block is edited in Content Builder. What happens to the emails that use it?
options: The block is duplicated for each email
Nothing until each email is republished
Only new emails pick up the change
They all reflect the change
sampleQuestions.explanation: Shared content is the point of Content Builder, and it means an edit propagates to everything using that block.
whyWrong: Blocks are referenced, not copied.
No republishing step is required for shared content.
Existing emails use the same shared block.

sampleQuestions.question: Which number does the delivered figure on a tracking report represent?
options: Sent minus bounces
Sent minus unsubscribes
The size of the audience before exclusions
Opens plus clicks
sampleQuestions.explanation: Delivered is what reached the mailbox, which is the sent total less anything that bounced.
whyWrong: Unsubscribes are recorded separately and do not reduce the delivered count.
Audience size before exclusions is larger than the sent total.
Opens and clicks are engagement measured against delivered.

sampleQuestions.question: What identifies a contact across channels in Marketing Cloud Engagement?
options: The journey version number
The record ID
The email address
The contact key
sampleQuestions.explanation: The contact key is the single identifier that ties a person's email, mobile and other channel records together.
whyWrong: Journey versions describe a journey, not a person.
Record IDs belong to core Salesforce, not Marketing Cloud contacts.
Email addresses change and are not the cross-channel identifier.

sampleQuestions.question: A marketer wants to let subscribers opt out of a monthly newsletter without losing transactional email. What should they set up?
options: A publication list for the newsletter
A second contact key for each subscriber
A separate Marketing Cloud account
A suppression list of all subscribers
sampleQuestions.explanation: Publication lists let subscribers opt out of one category of mail while continuing to receive others.
whyWrong: Duplicate contact keys would fragment the contact record.
A separate account is a disproportionate and expensive answer.
Suppressing everyone would stop all mail, which is the opposite of the goal.

sampleQuestions.question: What does a SQL Query activity in Automation Studio do with its results?
options: Emails them to the account owner
Displays them on screen for review
Writes them into a target data extension
Creates a new subscriber list automatically
sampleQuestions.explanation: Queries in Automation Studio are configured with a target data extension and write their output there.
whyWrong: Query results are not emailed by default.
There is no interactive results grid for a scheduled query activity.
The target is a data extension, not a list.

sampleQuestions.question: Which is the clearest sign that a journey should re-evaluate its entry source more often?
options: The account has a number of business units configured in it
New contacts qualify all day and should enter promptly
The journey has too many decision splits
The emails have low open rates
sampleQuestions.explanation: Entry source evaluation frequency controls how quickly newly qualifying contacts are picked up.
whyWrong: Business unit structure is unrelated to entry frequency.
The number of splits has nothing to do with entry evaluation.
Open rates are a content and audience problem.

sampleQuestions.question: A test send is run before a campaign. What is its purpose?
options: To check rendering and personalisation first
To create the tracking report
To count the audience
To warm up the account's dedicated sending IP address
sampleQuestions.explanation: Test sends exist so you can see the email as a subscriber would, with personalisation resolved, before committing.
whyWrong: Tracking is produced by the real send.
Audience counts are visible when the audience is selected.
IP warming is a deliverability exercise handled separately.

sampleQuestions.question: Which statement about soft bounces is correct?
options: They mark that address as being permanently undeliverable
They are temporary failures and the platform will retry
They are counted as delivered
They trigger an automatic unsubscribe
sampleQuestions.explanation: A soft bounce is a temporary condition such as a full mailbox, so delivery is attempted again.
whyWrong: Permanent failure describes a hard bounce.
A bounce of any kind is not a delivery.
Bounces and unsubscribes are separate events.
